messages:
Samir: Heads-up — after flipping MIG+time-slice on the west-eu GPU pool we've been seeing long pending times for small jobs and a bunch of eviction churn. Anyone else seeing this?
Emma: Yep saw it last night. Small inference pods (2-4 vCPU, tiny GPU slice) pile up while CA spins up full nodes.
Jake: Can you paste the pending pod message? is it Pending/Unschedulable or Pending/Provisioning?
Samir: Mostly 'Pending' with message '0/10 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't have free GPUs'. Then CA starts creating new nodes but they arrive ~2-4m later.
Yuna: That's the thing: with MIG + timeslicing we end up with fragmentation so scheduler can't pack slices efficiently. CA sees not enough allocatable GPU and provisions whole extra GPU nodes. Latency spike.
Emma: Also noticed kube-scheduler prefers exact matching device plugin annotations, so small-slice pods often wait for a node with appropriate slice profile.
Samir: infra-bot posted a node event dump earlier, here's a short grep I ran:```bash
kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep gpu
# shows new nodes provisioning (Provisioned) but allocatable.gpu remains 0 until device plugin ready
```
Jake: Two immediate levers we considered: (1) split node pools by mode (MIG-only vs time-slice-only) so scheduling is deterministic, (2) keep a small hot spare pool of pre-warmed nodes to hide provisioning latency.
Yuna: Agree on split pools. When both modes coexist in one pool CA's granularity is weird: it treats each node as a monolith and can't scale fractional GPUs.
Emma: Hot pool is expensive though. We should quantify idle GPU-hours vs reduced tail latency. Any recent metrics?
Samir: I pulled 24h numbers: pre-warmed pool (10 nodes) adds ~11% GPU-hours but cuts median pending->running from 3.5m to 30s for small jobs. Worth it for RL/real-time customers.
Jake: For cost sensitivity we can use preemptible instances for the hot pool and have a non-preemptible backup. Reduces cost but adds eviction complexity.
Yuna: Another idea: tune cluster-autoscaler expander and balance-similar-node-pools to favor pools that reduce fragmentation. Also increase `--scale-up-delay` or use CA scale-up buffer config so CA doesn't overprovision many nodes at once.
Emma: Can we improve scheduling by exposing finer-grained GPU resources via the device-plugin and using topology-aware scheduling? A couple of pods could share a GPU slice if we relax strict slice matching.
Samir: I tried a quick prototype toleration/nodeSelector approach:```yaml
nodeSelector:
  gpu.mode: timeslice
tolerations:
  - key: "gpu.mig"
    operator: "Exists"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
```
But that requires infra changes across helm charts and job templates.
Jake: Ops checklist proposal: 1) create two node pools (mig, timeslice) with labels; 2) add small hotpool timeslice preemptible nodes (3-5) behind autoscaler; 3) CA config: expander=least-waste, scaleUpDelay=10s, maxBulkScaling=2; 4) monitor pending queue metric and alert at 1m+ median.
Yuna: +1. Also add a rollout plan: migrate one non-critical namespace to timeslice pool first, run load test.
Emma: For visibility, can infra-bot surface a synthetic metric: pending_gpu_pods_count and average provisioning latency. Then link to runbook.
infra-bot: noted — will add metric and create Grafana panel under infra/gpu-provisioning. Created alert: pending_gpu_pods_count > 5 for 5m -> #oncall.
Samir: I'll prototype the pool split and hotpool (low-risk namespace). Jake can help with CA config and Yuna can run the load test. Emma will own the cost analysis.
Jake: I'll also test least-waste expander and see how CA behaves under bursty arrival patterns.
Yuna: If anyone wants the sample test harness I used (small pod generator + prom scrape), ping me and I'll drop it in eng-infra repo.
Emma: Thanks — sync in 2 days with results. :thumbsup:
